works.abstract: Global application of agricultural plastic mulch is increasing. While these films offer benefits for crop production, they also are a large source of plastic waste and pollution in both terrestrial and aquatic systems. The current scale of global mulch application and its deleterious impacts are unclear. Current estimates of agricultural plastic use remain limited by field-specific growing patterns and data limitations. Satellite spectroscopy may offer a means to reduce this uncertainty and model agricultural plastic use on large spatial and temporal scales, though temporally variable crop canopy growth and spectrally diverse plastic targets complicate this approach. To build toward improved plasticulture estimates, this study presents an interpretable, spectral-based classification of bulk plastic use in a California agricultural site using Sentinel-2 imagery. In situ reflectance measurements of soil and white, green, and black plastic mulch endmembers were collected using a Spectra Vista Corporation HR-1024i Spectroradiometer from 350–2500 nm. A combination of field observations and high spatial resolution NearMap imagery (n = 416 spectra) were compiled and divided into 60% training and 40% testing data using a stratified sampling approach. Informed by field reflectance data, mixture analyses, and Sentinel-2 reflectance imagery, an empirical decision tree classification was parameterized to classify dark and bright plastic debris from soil and crop (accuracy = 0.982, kappa coefficient = 0.973, macro-averaged F1-score = 0.967). Modeled agricultural plastic distributions were then retrieved through a time series of Sentinel-2 imagery over Santa Maria, CA, from April 2023 to January 2025, elucidating patterns in plastic application and crop canopy growth without the need for prior knowledge of field growing and management patterns. These results are encouraging for the utility of optical remote sensing in modeling plastic use patterns and identifying contamination hotspots throughout California and, potentially, similarly mulched agroecological systems.
works.title: Remote estimation of plastic distribution in California agriculture using Sentinel-2 imagery: a case study

works.abstract: Agricultural plastics have become deeply embedded within modern farming systems, where they enhance productivity, efficiency, and crop quality. However, they also generate environmental concerns related to waste accumulation, disposal challenges, and ecosystem pollution. Despite growing attention to agricultural plastic pollution, relatively little is known about farmers' perceptions of these materials or how views vary across different farming contexts. This study examines California strawberry growers' perceptions of agricultural plastics using data from a survey of 126 farm operators, farm managers, and other agricultural decision-makers. Exploratory factor analysis identified four distinct dimensions of agricultural plastic perceptions: plastic utility, plastic stewardship, plastic reduction, and plastic harm. Associations between these perceptions and farm structure, production practices, marketing channels, environmental orientation, and grower demographics are then examined. Results indicate that growers more embedded within intensive commercial strawberry systems tend to view plastics as more useful and less in need of reduction. In contrast, growers more oriented toward organic production, direct-to-consumer marketing, and environmental stewardship express stronger concern about plastic harm and greater support for reducing plastic use. At the same time, even growers expressing strong environmental concern continued to recognize the functional necessity of plastics within strawberry production, suggesting a “love-hate relationship” surrounding agricultural plastics. Efforts to reduce agricultural plastic pollution will therefore likely require structural and infrastructural changes rather than relying solely on voluntary shifts in farmers’ perceptions and behaviors.
works.title: A love-hate relationship: Strawberry growers’ perceptions of agricultural plastics in California, USA
